catalog_quote: 2.2.1. STRESS IN INHERENTLY STRESSED ROOTS. The vast majority of native-vocabulary Cupeño roots exhibit inherent stress. When these inherently stressed roots appear in construction with prefixes and suffixes, stress remains on the inherently stressed syllable of the root. Most inherently stressed Cupeño words are stressed on the first syllable of the root. However, I have identified 204 non-derived words that are stressed on the second syllable or later. These are listed in Appendix A. Only six words ... are attested with stress on the third syllable or later. ... It seems most likely that Cupeño has simply lost phonological vowel length in non-initial stressed syllables, since the stress itself carries the necessary information and makes length redundant. ... 2.2.2. sweep_summary: All four works with stress in the title are about Cupeño word stress. Alderete 2001 (open ROA-253 preprint, already held by the project) was read: root accent overrides affix accent, rightmost accented affix wins with unaccented roots, default word-initial stress otherwise — confirms the catalog's lexical coding (Hill 2005). Yates 2017 (UCLA diss., held by the project, extra item) refines the rule to a leftmost-accent/BAP statement, reports no secondary stress and no weight effect, still lexical. Hill & Hill 1968 (DOI 10.1086/465023), Munro 1990 (10.1086/466151) and Mamet 2011 (10.1086/659737) are all IJAL/UChicago paywalled with no repository copies (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, archive.org SIM, CORE/BASE checked; UChicago/JSTOR landing pages 403); their content is known only secondhand (Hill 2005:25 quotes Munro's Pre-Cupeño long-vowel-else-initial rule; Yates quotes Hill & Hill 1968:236-237 on no secondary stress and length irrelevance; Mamet 2011:250 n.4 agrees on length). Nothing read contradicts the catalog; Hill 2005 remains the deciding source. for the session was exhausted, so discovery relied on API and direct downloads.

new_statements.reading: Lexical accent: primary stress sits on the inherently accented syllable of the root (contrastively 1st or 2nd syllable of the root); if the root is unaccented, the rightmost accented affix (person prefix or suffix -qál/-qá/-í) takes it; if nothing in the word is accented, the word-initial syllable is stressed by default. Confirms the catalog's lexical coding and its affix-governed secondary rule, and states the default-to-initial explicitly. It is an analysis built on Hill's data, not fieldwork, so it does not displace Hill 2005.

sources.citation: Alderete, John D. 2001. Root-controlled accent in Cupeño. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 19(3): 455-502.
sources.quote: [§3.1 p.8] Summarizing the above discussion in synchronic terms, one key observation governing the distribution of stress in roots is that long vowels attract stress. In contrast to this predictable part of the stress system, stress is contrastive in roots which do not contain long vowels: stress may fall on either the first or second syllable ... [§4.1 p.13-14] when an inherently accented affix combines with an accented root, root accent always prevails. ... (27) Summary of Cupeño Accent: If the root contains an inherently accented vowel, that vowel receives primary stress ... In words with unaccented roots, the rightmost accented vowel in an affix bears the primary stress ... If the word does not contain an inherently accented morpheme, the first vowel of the word receives the primary stress
sources.locator: ROA-253 preprint §3.1 'The Data' p.8; §4.1 'Data and Observations' pp.10-14, summary (27) p.14 (published NLLT pp. 455-502)
sources.note: Canonical lexical-accent analysis (data from Hill 1967, Hill & Hill 1968, Hill & Nolasquez 1973, Crowhurst 1994 and Jane Hill's fieldnotes): (i) roots carry inherent accent, contrastive between 1st and 2nd syllable in short-vowel roots (post-peninitial stress rare, n.14); (ii) root accent overrides affix accent; (iii) with unaccented roots the rightmost accented affix (person prefixes né-/pé-/chém- etc., suffixes -qál, -qá, -í) is stressed, and a stressed prefix can be non-initial (mi-né-tew); (iv) with no accented morpheme, default initial stress (yáx-em). sources.citation: Yates, Anthony D. 2017. Against Root Faithfulness in Cupeño Stress. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 4. doi:10.3765/amp.v4i0.3986
sources.quote: Word stress in Cupeño — an extinct Uto-Aztecan language previously spoken in southern California (Hill 2005; cf. Golla 2011) — is FREE, CULMINATIVE, OBLIGATORY, and UNBOUNDED (Hyman 2006, van der Hulst 2014, i.a.). Every word bears a single primary stress, realized principally by increased duration and intensity of the stressed syllable. Stress typically falls within the first three syllables of the word, most frequently on the initial syllable of the root, but second syllable root stress is common. In addition, a few longer words have stress on the third syllable of the root or later, which suggests that there are no window restrictions on word stress. [...] Stress is instead attracted to certain morphemes, which are lexically marked as preferred hosts of prosodic prominence, i.e. accented. [n. 3:] It is generally held that Cupeño lacks secondary stress (cf. Alderete, 2001b:458 n.4).
sources.locator: p. 2, sec. 2.1 and n. 3; abstract; p. 9, sec. 5
sources.note: Optimality-theoretic analysis of Cupeño word stress: primary stress falls on the leftmost lexically accented morpheme, else on the word's left edge, arguing against root-faithfulness accounts.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology

sources.citation: Yates, Anthony D. 2017. Lexical Accent in Cupeño, Hittite, and Indo-European. PhD dissertation, UCLA. Ch. 2 'Analyzing Lexical Accent in Cupeño', pp. 41-?
sources.quote: Cupeño is a lexical-accent system; against Alderete's root-controlled accent, 'the distribution of primary stress in Cupeño is consistent with Kiparsky and Halle's (1977) BASIC ACCENTUATION PRINCIPLE: If a word has more than one accented vowel, the leftmost of these receives word stress. If a word has no accented vowel, the leftmost syllable receives word stress.'
sources.locator: ch. 2, pp. 41-42 (BAP statement, ex. 26); data from Hill & Nolasquez 1973 and Hill 2005
sources.note: Reanalysis of Alderete: Cupeño stress follows the Basic Accentuation Principle (leftmost lexically accented morpheme, else word-initial); person prefixes are unaccented and get default left-edge stress; no secondary stress; unbounded; vowel length plays no role. Data from Hill & Nolasquez 1973 and Hill 2005. Confirms lexical and refines the rule statement (leftmost-accent rather than root-control), consistent with Hill 2005's 'prefixes are stressed unless a stressed or stress-attracting suffix is present'.

sources.quote: Cupeno has a fairly unusual synchronic stress system, according to the analysis of Hill and Hill (1968): most roots have first- or second-syllable stress lexically marked, and there are certain suffixes which have the effect of causing stress to fall on the last vowel of a preceding root. In addition, there is a small set of "stressless" roots with no inherently marked stress: a word containing one of these is stressed initially (on the first syllable of the root, or on a prefix, if present) unless it contains one of the stress-attracting suffixes.
sources.locator: printed p. 313 (PDF 315); Table 2 p. 307: 'Lexical, Hill & Hill 1968'
sources.note: Second-hand (cites Hill & Hill 1968). Catalog classification lexical (Hill 2005): agrees. p. 315 adds that the unaffixed Cupeno stressless roots all have long initial vowels, which receive stress (read by Munro as a relic of second-mora stress). p. 319: main stress only on first or second syllable. No secondary stress, no tone, not instrumental.
sources.venue: Studies in Stress and Accent (Southern California Occasional Papers in Linguistics 4)

sources.quote: [secondhand, Hill 2005:25] Munro (1990) argues that Proto-Cupan— the Takic community ancestral to Cupeño, Cahuilla, and Luiseño—exhibited a quantity-sensitive stress rule, which is still observed in Luiseño. The “Pre-Cupeño” form of the stress rule was A. If there is a long vowel in the first or second syllable, stress it. B. If not, stress the first syllable (Munro 1990:225). [StressTyp2 passage 849, attributed to Munro 1990] Stress is usually initial. In some words a vowel other than the first used to be long and bear main stress. This vowel length has been reduced in Cupeno but the stress remains on the original syllable. In such cases stress is lexical.

sources.quote: [secondhand, Yates 2017:41] Cupeño has roots and affixes that are “inherently stressed” or “[inherently] stressless”, as well as affixes that “place the stress on the last vowel of [a stressless] root”; the single surface prosodic prominence (STRESS) is assigned to a syllable that is “inherently stressed” (or pre-stressed), or in the absence of one, to the word’s initial syllable. [Yates 2017:53 n.24] Hill and Hill (1968: 237) ... state that “long vowels have no relation with the rules for stress placement”. [Yates 2017:43] There is no secondary stress in Cupeño, or at least no audible manifestation thereof (Hill and Hill 1968: 236)
